claims.text: The retained VSS releases show active evolution of the common vehicle-data model and its tooling, including schema/ID generation, struct support, overlays/profiles, motion-management/health signals and deliberate backward-incompatible cleanup.
claims.context: Synthesis of release notes across major/minor versions.

claims.text: V4.2 adds struct support for DDS IDL generation together with JSON Schema and identifier-generation tooling.
claims.context: Direct release-note entries relevant to typed data contracts and interface generation.

claims.text: V6.0 explicitly documents multiple backward-incompatible signal/unit changes and removal of the OBD branch.

limitations.text: VSS specifies a vehicle-data taxonomy/model and associated tooling; these releases do not by themselves establish a transport protocol, service runtime, or OEM-wide adoption.

targets.target: Verify the release date, material technical changes and maturity significance of v4.1; distinguish release existence from maintainer/project claims.
targets.finding: Release notes introduce quantity files/unit syntax updates, new signals and vss-tools support for static IDs and JSON Schema.

targets.target: Verify the release date, material technical changes and maturity significance of v4.2; distinguish release existence from maintainer/project claims.
targets.finding: Release notes add new signal areas plus struct support in vspec2ddsidl, a JSON Schema generator and an ID generator.

targets.target: Verify the release date, material technical changes and maturity significance of v5.0; distinguish release existence from maintainer/project claims.
targets.finding: Release notes remove UUIDs from standard release artifacts by default, deprecate the OBD branch, improve overlay support and refactor tooling.

targets.target: Verify the release date, material technical changes and maturity significance of v5.1; distinguish release existence from maintainer/project claims.
targets.finding: Release notes add/adjust motion-management and seat-related signals and include VSS Extension Profile documentation work.

targets.target: Verify the release date, material technical changes and maturity significance of v6.0; distinguish release existence from maintainer/project claims.
targets.finding: Release notes remove the OBD branch, add pattern/default support, change units and several signal definitions including backward-incompatible changes, and add vehicle-health-management signals.

editorial.why_now_note: The series spans late 2023 to early 2026 and shows a common data-contract layer maturing while SDV ecosystems converge on reusable vehicle semantics.
editorial.rationale: Strong data-contract candidate that complements middleware/network evidence and makes the service/data separation explicit.

claims.text: Across retained 3.5.0–3.7.5 releases, vSomeIP shows continuing work on routing/service discovery, endpoint architecture, concurrency/race robustness, platform portability and test infrastructure.
claims.context: Synthesis of project-authored release notes; not a claim of independent conformance or deployment maturity.

claims.text: The 3.7.0 notes include a client/server endpoint architecture rework and fully atomic offer/stop-service operations.
The 3.7.5 notes include support for multiple major-version offerings and broad routing-command/IPC refactoring.

limitations.text: Release notes establish project changes, not independent SOME/IP conformance, production deployment scale, safety qualification or comparative performance.

targets.target: Verify the release date, material technical changes and maturity significance of vSomeIP-Lib 3.5.0; distinguish release existence from maintainer/project claims.
targets.finding: Release notes add lazy policy loading, event debouncing/selective events, SOME/IP-TP remote-address rework, security-configuration separation for applications in one process, and reliability fixes.

targets.target: Verify the release date, material technical changes and maturity significance of vSomeIP-Lib 3.6.0; distinguish release existence from maintainer/project claims.
targets.finding: Release notes drop vsomeip2 compatibility and include endpoint/routing/service-subscription synchronization, suspend/resume/network-change and test-harness work.

targets.target: Verify the release date, material technical changes and maturity significance of vSomeIP-Lib 3.7.0; distinguish release existence from maintainer/project claims.
targets.finding: Release notes include endpoint client/server restructuring, atomic offer/stop-service operations, connection control, service-discovery reliability fixes and substantial robustness/test work.

targets.target: Verify the release date, material technical changes and maturity significance of vSomeIP-Lib 3.7.2; distinguish release existence from maintainer/project claims.
targets.finding: Release notes introduce hybrid mode and further separate/decouple endpoint/routing structures while addressing data races and service-discovery/routing synchronization.

targets.target: Verify the release date, material technical changes and maturity significance of vSomeIP-Lib 3.7.3; distinguish release existence from maintainer/project claims.
targets.finding: Release notes upgrade the project to C++20 and continue endpoint, service-discovery and routing synchronization/refactoring plus reliability/test work.

targets.target: Verify the release date, material technical changes and maturity significance of vSomeIP-Lib 3.7.5; distinguish release existence from maintainer/project claims.
targets.finding: Release notes include multiple-major-version offerings, routing IPC/command refactoring, provider/consumer error separation, portability and extensive race/robustness/test improvements.

editorial.why_now_note: The release series spans October 2024 through August 2026 and provides an implementation-level view of a major open SOME/IP middleware stack evolving alongside SDV architecture changes.
editorial.rationale: Useful maturity/implementation trajectory for the runtime layer when kept distinct from standardization and deployment claims.

claims.context: Consortium architectural framing, not a normative interoperability guarantee.

targets.target: Verify the official scope/status and architecture-significant statements on covesa-vsomeip; distinguish directly checkable facts from organization/project claims.
targets.finding: The official COVESA page establishes vSomeIP project scope, SOME/IP implementation role and its relationship to VSS; adoption scale is deliberately not upgraded to an independent fact.

editorial.why_now_note: A concrete open SOME/IP middleware implementation is directly relevant to the service-oriented runtime layer of centralized/zonal E/E architectures.
editorial.rationale: Provides implementation-level evidence that complements protocol/specification discussion without equating project-host claims with independent adoption proof.

sources.title: Automotive Middleware Performance: Comparison of FastDDS, Zenoh and vSomeIP
sources.role: Author v2 paper used to verify test metrics, centralized/distributed topology setup, middleware findings, network-stack contribution and explicit experiment exclusions.

claims.text: The study compares FastDDS, Zenoh and vSomeIP using time-to-first-message, steady-state communication time, latency decomposition, message loss, scaling and resource usage across centralized and Ethernet-distributed topologies and several sensor-message profiles.
The authors report Zenoh as fastest to first message, FastDDS close behind, and vSomeIP substantially slower, especially in larger/distributed topologies.
claims.context: Finding from the tested configurations only.

claims.text: For D1-1 IMU best-effort communication, the paper reports roughly 0.487 ms for FastDDS, 3.170 ms for Zenoh, and 7.817 ms for vSomeIP; behavior varies with topology and data rate.
claims.context: One concrete test configuration; not a universal middleware ranking.

claims.text: The authors find that kernel/network-stack processing contributes more than half of end-to-end latency for FastDDS and Zenoh in the examined D1-1 setup and is even larger for vSomeIP reliable mode.

metrics.context: D1-1 instrumented experiment; the paper reports about 0.35-0.37 ms from kernel/network stack.

limitations.text: Results are configuration- and Linux-testbed-specific; the authors identify embedded-platform evaluation as future work.

Two configurations were omitted as not meaningful: vSomeIP best-effort above the small-message case because SOME/IP-TP was not implemented, and Zenoh reliable because the selected reliable configuration did not affect transmission.
The paper itself shows topology/data-rate dependent reversals, so its measurements should not be generalized into a single universal middleware ranking.

targets.target: Verify the architecture, evaluation setup, material claims and limitations reported for Automotive Middleware Performance: Comparison of FastDDS, Zenoh and vSomeIP; preserve paper results as AUTHOR_CLAIM unless independently established.
targets.finding: The v2 paper provides a concrete multi-topology measurement methodology, detailed discovery/latency/message-loss/resource findings, kernel instrumentation and explicit excluded configurations. Reported measurements remain AUTHOR_CLAIM tied to the testbed.

editorial.why_now_note: The paper directly quantifies middleware and OS/network-stack trade-offs that become important when SDV functions move onto central HPCs and Ethernet-distributed zones.
editorial.rationale: Strong comparative evidence for the communication/runtime layer, provided measurements are presented with topology/testbed boundaries.

sources.title: CARISMA: CAR-Integrated Service Mesh Architecture
sources.role: Author paper used to verify the multi-HPC service-mesh architecture, proof-of-concept setup, runtime relocation behavior, and evaluation boundary.

claims.text: CARISMA adapts the service-mesh pattern to multiple interlinked automotive HPCs, with a central Control Plane, one proxy per HPC, node/service registries, and location-transparent service routing.
The architecture can model a cloud backend as another registered node/service endpoint so in-vehicle callers use the same proxy-mediated service mechanism.
claims.context: Architecture capability described by the authors.

claims.text: A proof of concept on two private-networked virtual machines used Go, gRPC, Envoy, a Control Plane, registries, orchestrator and three software components; the authors demonstrated communication across nodes and relocation of a service without reconfiguring its caller.

limitations.text: Validation is a two-VM proof of concept rather than embedded automotive HPC hardware or an in-vehicle network.
The authors explicitly defer a sound evaluation of CARISMA overhead versus direct inter-service communication to future work.
The prototype intentionally uses exactly one proxy per HPC and does not claim redundant proxy behavior.

targets.target: Verify the architecture, evaluation setup, material claims and limitations reported for CARISMA: CAR-Integrated Service Mesh Architecture; preserve paper results as AUTHOR_CLAIM unless independently established.
targets.finding: The primary paper establishes the multi-HPC service-mesh design and a two-VM proof-of-concept feasibility test, while explicitly leaving communication-overhead evaluation for future work.

unresolved_questions: What latency, jitter, CPU/memory overhead and failure-mode behavior would CARISMA exhibit on automotive HPC hardware and deterministic in-vehicle networks?

editorial.why_now_note: CARISMA directly explores the runtime/service-routing consequences of distributing software across multiple automotive HPCs, a central issue in centralized/zonal SDV architectures.
editorial.rationale: Strong architecture-pattern evidence for separating service location from application logic, with clear prototype limitations that can be carried into comparison.

artifact.canonical_name: AUTOSAR AP and ROS 2 Collaboration Framework

sources.title: AUTOSAR AP and ROS 2 Collaboration Framework
sources.role: Author arXiv paper/preprint used to verify the architecture, evaluation scope, material claims, and limitations available in the primary text.

claims.text: The proposed framework implements a ROS 2-side bridge that converts between DDS and SOME/IP, including SOME/IP service discovery and type conversion, to connect ROS 2 nodes with AUTOSAR Adaptive applications.
The framework includes automatic generation of FIDL/FDEPL configuration from a small set of service/message identifiers and can derive conversion specifications for custom ROS 2 messages.

The paper evaluates the bridge using ROS 2 Humble/Fast DDS and vsomeip on two Ubuntu PCs, and an AUTOSAR Adaptive R20-11/QNX environment running in QEMU; seven PointCloud2 data sizes are used for latency evaluation.

metrics.name: generated PointCloud2 conversion file length
metrics.context: Example reported for sensor_msgs::msg::PointCloud2 configuration generation.

metrics.name: PointCloud2 data sizes evaluated
metrics.context: Latency evaluation varies the number of point-cloud points across seven data sizes.

limitations.text: AUTOSAR Adaptive/QNX is evaluated in QEMU rather than on an automotive target ECU/HPC.
The implementation/evaluation is tied to ROS 2 Humble, Fast DDS, vsomeip 3.4.9.1 and AUTOSAR Adaptive R20-11; interoperability across other implementations/releases requires separate evidence.

targets.target: Verify the architecture, evaluation setup, material claims and limitations reported for AUTOSAR AP and ROS 2 Collaboration Framework; preserve paper results as AUTHOR_CLAIM unless independently established.
targets.finding: The full primary text verifies the DDS-SOME/IP bridge architecture, automatic configuration generation, software versions, QEMU AUTOSAR environment, and seven-size PointCloud2 latency methodology.

editorial.why_now_note: Bridging AUTOSAR Adaptive/SOME-IP and ROS 2/DDS directly addresses mixed-platform SDV development and reuse rather than forcing one middleware stack everywhere.
editorial.rationale: Strong middleware-boundary evidence: it demonstrates a concrete conversion/configuration architecture and realistic development tooling, with the QEMU/vendor/version boundary retained.
